payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
A signing key can be stolen. Every provenance system built on signatures inherits that sentence, and most inherit the answer along with it: revocation, the practice of publicly declaring a key dead so nothing it signs is trusted again. The word comes from the web's certificate infrastructure, where it has worked for decades. It does not transfer cleanly, and the failure is worth walking through, because it sits at the center of any permanent record built on keys.

The fork

Declaring a key dead forces a decision about everything it signed while it lived, and the two available answers fail in opposite directions.

A · Void everything

The archive falls with the key

The compromise voids the key, the key made the records, so a decade of legitimate work signed before the thief appeared falls with it.

B · Honor what came before

The forgeries come with it

A stolen key signs exactly as well as an owned one, and nothing inside a signature says when it was really produced.

A thief holding the key can date a record to any year he likes, with no additional effort, so honoring what came before admits every one of those records too.

Neither branch leaves the archive intact, and the archive is the entire product. A payment system, a court, or a platform consulting the record ten years out has no interest in the key's biography. It needs to know whether one specific record from years back still holds.

Why the web's fix inverts

The web met the same fork and dissolved it through expiry. Certificates now live for months and are headed toward weeks, so a stolen one usually dies of old age before an attacker gets full value from it. Expiry works there because a web certificate asserts a fact about the present: this server, right now, is the one it claims to be. When the assertion lapses, nothing worth keeping lapses with it.

A creation-time signature asserts a fact about a moment that has already passed and will not recur. Expiring it destroys the one thing it exists to preserve. The same mechanism, moved from one system to the other, performs the opposite of its function.

The date does the work

What narrows the fork is a clock the signer does not control. A signature dated only by its own author proves nothing about when it was made, since the author, or whoever holds the author's key, writes the date. An anchor placed by an independent clock gives the record a position in time that a later thief cannot forge backward. The anchoring can take several forms, from a timestamping authority to a public chain, and the differences matter less than the property they share: the signer cannot move the clock.

Once every legitimate record carries such an anchor, a compromise stops being a verdict on the key's whole history and becomes a boundary. Records anchored before the compromise date stand. Anything after it falls. Revocation shrinks from an amputation to a cut at a known line, and the line is only as trustworthy as the clock that drew it.

The anchor has to exist before anyone needs it. A record that skipped anchoring at creation cannot be anchored retroactively in any form a dispute will respect, for the same reason the rest of the record is recorded at the moment a work is made or never recorded at all.

One piece stays unsolved. The web keeps its death notices in registries run by certificate authorities, entities whose business is being findable. Music has no registrar for dead keys, and a revocation nobody can look up protects nobody. Somebody has to maintain the list, and the obvious candidates, the distributors and the collecting societies, are the institutions a signing model was supposed to route around. That is a governance problem, and the mathematics has nothing to say about it.
payload.title: Revocation unsigns nothing
